## 12 February, year 2672 since the Creation of the World

How glad I am to be here at last, in the capital, studying at the Ardebrig academy, the world's centre of art and science.

A little about myself: though I descend from one of our kings, a dozen other kinsmen stand between me and any claim to the throne. Power, however, has never interested me. My true passion has always been books. Reading everything I could lay my hands on, I went through my parents' entire library, including not only elven works such as "The Power of Oberon", which tells of the palace intrigues that erupted when the one who is now a Great Mage, and was once a king, renounced the crown.

Or, for instance, I read "The Secrets of Ker-Is by Night", a somewhat frivolous tale of an elven maiden pursued by a bloodthirsty werewolf, and I mastered works describing the lives of other races, such as "Nefertiti and Akhenaten: In the Name of Love", a rather amusing story written by an eyewitness in the last days of Hickut.

I even came by works like "Mechanisation. Volume 3", filled with repulsive details of what that people did to themselves in their attempt to gain immortality.

In my wanderings through the lines of dusty treatises, my faithful companion was my cousin, or, to be precise, my second cousin, Elined.

Oh, Elined, even now, as I write these lines, I see your finely chiselled profile bent over a new folio.

You shared my passion, devouring this knowledge alongside me. It was this very path that brought us here.

Reality has surpassed all my expectations: the libraries of Ker-Is exceed everything I have seen until now. Such a multitude of folios, grimoires and incunabula deserves the closest study. But where to begin?

Without a plan I am doomed to be buried under a mountain of unsorted information, so it is very important to think through what we will take up first. I want to discuss it with Elined; she has always been distinguished by rigorous judgement and a rational approach.

Otherwise, life goes on as usual. I have been presented to our king, a distant relative of mine. The reign of Dernier began not so very long ago, right after the extinction of the previous dynasty, the Velund, from which that same Oberon who renounced the throne descends.

The capital is full of other noble houses too, many of whom pride themselves on their antiquity.

Here, it would seem, one might turn to politics, to relations with the other elven Houses that have founded states of their own; I find that subject rather dull, however.

The reasons for this are simple: the borders of Irene are securely closed by a magical barrier, and those who now reside in the capital are for the most part gilded youth who do not know what to do with themselves. And what could they say about those who live outside?

We, protected by the power of our ancestors from any interference from without, live for the most part in blissful ignorance. All that is left to us is books.

Well, it only remains to find Elined so that we can discuss our prospects, what we want to take up in the near future. Strange, but my cousin has not been seen for a long while...

## 1 June, year 2672 since the Creation of the World

Oh, what an unhappy day! I never thought such a thing could ever happen.

My Elined, what has become of you? How could you renounce our ideals, everything you and I dreamed of, everything we discussed for so long in our library?

The capital is a wonderful place for all who hold knowledge dear, but even here there is no shortage of ruinous places for those who yield to the temptations of an easy life, full of momentary pleasures and empty amusements.

I found my cousin in one such establishment, bearing the name, oh great powers, "Whips and Chains"... There she was making merry, dancing and singing in the company of some good-for-nothings from among those very young scions of the noble Houses. I could only gaze in astonishment as the one I had revered as the cleverest of women in this world kissed some blue-haired flirt full on the mouth, while at the same time offering her unlaced bodice to one of the dandies.

I was simply at a loss for words at such a sight, and only after waiting and catching my breath did I pull myself together and stride firmly towards my merrily laughing cousin. Seizing her by the sleeve, I drew her aside to talk. Here, I must admit, my composure failed me, and I shouted at Elined with all my heart, voicing all my indignation.

I told her everything I thought of her behaviour; she told me everything she thought of mine. And so, word by word, we arrived at some very inelegant insults, when we realised that everyone in the hall was watching us. In parting I received a stinging slap, after which I found no other way out but to leave. In anger I walked through the narrow streets of Ker-Is, not understanding myself where exactly I was going.

My anger was boundless, for I had been betrayed by the one I considered my most reliable ally, the one I had seen at my side in our future endeavours.

A sudden thought came to me, like a flash of lightning. What is the matter? Why are we elves like this? Most of us see nothing else for ourselves but a life of endless pleasures, yet it was not always so. Once our ancestors waged long wars against the world around us, wishing to make this kingdom the safest and most beautiful place in the world. They were far stronger than we are, and lived in far more dangerous times. Their labours have not vanished without a trace; they still surround every inhabitant of the kingdom.

But their descendants have grown much weaker. Pampered. Spineless. But what is the reason? What happened to my people that they changed so? I had no answers, nor were there any in the books I had read before. In them the past was always likened to a forgotten dream, of which only vague sensations remained. Why have we forgotten where we came from? Why do none of our historical works touch upon anything older than a few centuries? And who knows the truth? The Great Mages? I cannot even say with certainty how old they themselves are, but I know that they are now immortal...

Now all of this seemed to me far more important than my frivolous cousin.

## 13 July, year 2672 since the Creation of the World

In search of answers to my questions, I went to the royal library. As a distant kinsman of the king, I had full access to all the archives, even the most ancient. But were there any archives at all? The chamberlain accompanying me, who had been charged with giving me due assistance, unlocked long-closed doors that, it seemed, had not been opened for decades, if not longer. I found myself in dusty rooms where stacks of papers lay in disorder on ancient tables. What a striking contrast with the order in which the main halls are kept, crammed with entertaining, romantic and magical literature. The past of the elves had been thoroughly forgotten.

Sitting down at one of the tables, I began sorting through the papers. Indeed, some of what lay before me were old chronicles, some were records of the palace's needs. But both were of the utmost importance. Alas, the further into the past, the less reliable its traces. Ink fades, paper crumbles into scraps, and of the testimonies of what once was, only dust remains.

Realising that a long task lay ahead, I decided to request an audience with the king. The position of his distant kinsman had its advantages, and I intended to make use of them.

Well, my venture was crowned with success. I managed both to enrol at Ardebrig and to obtain the post of court historian. When I set out my plan to the king, the faces of those around fell. Now, apparently, I am considered an eccentric, if not worse. But I intend, step by step, to get to the bottom of our history, for who are we without what shaped our path in the past?

Every day I trained under the masters of the magical art; every evening I went to the wing of the royal palace given over to me and sorted through the archives that had fallen to my lot.

I very quickly gained the reputation of a rather strange elf who refused the customary pleasures and amusements. I was sent invitations to Balls, and I threw them into the wastepaper basket; I was summoned to yet another important dinner, and I shrugged and returned to my work. My cousin, as far as I could gather from the whispers of my fellow students, had become a very popular person who enjoyed universal adoration, but I did not care. I did not seek to meet her, and the letters she sent me I simply burned unread.

## 2 February, year 2674 since the Creation of the World

So a year passed, and then another. Having finished with the royal archive, I asked the king to issue an order to our Houses that they bring all their old manuscripts and other papers to the new library I had organised.

He was obeyed without any objection, the matter being considered a rather strange whim. For the most part my kinsfolk went on ignoring what I was doing, but in some an interest did arise after all. History in itself still seemed dull to them, but they found in it ideas for their works, drew inspiration from what was described there, devising new paintings and architectural plans, and sought the means of settling ancient lawsuits.

My studies of magic went well: I quickly passed through the degrees of initiation as adept and acolyte, becoming at last a magister. All my free time I continued to spend on the library, gradually moving from putting old manuscripts in order to composing a work of my own. But many difficulties arose along this path, above all because our history remained tragically incomplete. Only fragmentary records bore witness to what had taken place before the Transformation. I found myself at a dead end from which I could as yet see no way out. To tie the scattered threads of history together, I needed to find someone who knew more.

In these gloomy thoughts I was pacing the halls of my library when my gaze fell, quite by chance, on one of the visitors, or rather a woman visitor, bent over one of the volumes. The most unusual thing was that she was not an elf. Before me, beyond any doubt, was a child of the human race. Golden-red hair, delicate features. She was beautiful in her own way. I resolved to speak to her.

"Good day," I greeted her, sitting down at the same table. "Perhaps I can help you with something? The thing is, I am the royal librarian, and, in all modesty, I know the contents of this library better than anyone."

She raised her green eyes to me. Beautiful, she possessed not the ideal beauty that distinguished the elves, yet at the same time something young, fresh and unusual emanated from her.

The human girl, noticing the interest in my eyes, smiled.

"Hello. Yes, perhaps you could help me. I was sent here by the sorceress Maeve, the keeper of Rahl-Ulrir. I would like to find information about my own past."

My confusion and incomprehension must have shown on my face, for the girl hastened to explain:

"My problem is that I do not remember my past. I have lived for more than a hundred years, and apparently I am immortal, but I know nothing of where I come from or who my relatives are... If your library holds any information, I would like to have it."

A riddle indeed. I pondered. Our history is full of vague legends about ancient heroes, about warriors of old, about wanderers who roamed the world... Perhaps there is something about this sorceress too. Gathering my thoughts, I nodded.

"I will help you. I think that together we can solve this mystery. But... how should I address you?"

She tilted her head slightly to one side:

"They call me Bindweed."

## 9 September, year 2678 since the Creation of the World

The longer we live, the less power time has over us. The years quicken their pace, one, another, a third... I myself did not notice how they ran by. Looking back, I understand that it was the happiest time of my life. I had work I loved, I had someone who understood me, I had no responsibilities. I simply lived and enjoyed it.

Bindweed proved to be a good helper. Together we accomplished a great deal, going through every archive there was in Irene. People whispered about us almost openly, but I paid no attention. Unlike many women of my race, this eternally young enchantress was far cleverer and more perceptive.

I tried to help her in every way I could, but in this matter she did far more than I.

There were monstrous gaps in her memory, created by magic of such an order that it is frightening even to imagine. Her first memory was of some field of death, and, if I understood her correctly, it was that very slaughter in which the last of the Hickutians perished.

Bindweed could not tell what exactly had happened there. She remembered only a strange sensation of monstrous darkness, the breath of death itself. She managed to do something so that this contagion would not spread further, and afterwards she buried all the fallen, dragging them away from the sinister Pyramid. One of the dead she remembered especially well, a young warrior in a white mask. She managed to drag them into empty tombs and then sealed the place with magic.

Then she set off north. She met many unusual things along the way, and visited a city high in the mountains, with many tall towers, where some unfortunate people lived who had fled from an unimaginable monster. She believed them and went to seek out the monster, wishing to be rid of it for ever. But on meeting it she again felt the same darkness and, taking fright, fled.

For a long time she wandered through the mountains, saw new inhabitants come to the ruins of abandoned cities, lived among them, then left and went on. So it went until her path crossed that of the Great Mages. But they had seen a great deal and, not particularly surprised by anything, sent her further on. That is how she came to be in Irene.

## 11 November, year 2688 since the Creation of the World

The years passed, and it became ever clearer to us that sooner or later we would have to leave Irene. It was too safe, too unchanging and too sleepy. Real history was being made beyond its borders. I had achieved here everything I could achieve, and it was time to move on. At the same time, I understood that, most likely, our paths would part.

I was close to completing my work, and, sitting by the fireplace, Bindweed read passages from it aloud:

"I cannot vouch for the accuracy of the information I have set down. Time flows like a dark river, and the beginning of history lies hidden in its depths. Much has been forgotten, and still more has been lost. All that remains to us are scraps of old documents and vague memories of what once was."

I sat and listened as she read. The past had always been a riddle to me, and I felt that this mystery was something fateful for all of us. Bindweed spoke of years gone by, of other peoples, of a past in which so much was unknown.

"Thus, after the Change, the history of the elves began anew. The past was left behind, becoming a half-forgotten, happy childhood dream. The elves, on awakening, began their life almost from a clean slate. They tried to forget their former aspirations, surrendering themselves wholly to the present. They were no longer interested in the deeds of their ancestors, their past feats or the chronicles of the War for Beauty. All of that had become meaningless and unnecessary.

That is why there are so many blank spots in the history of the world and the history of the elves. But this is all we have, and there is no one who could tell of the past more than the ancient elven manuscripts of my library, so few of which have survived."

"Maeve could," Bindweed said thoughtfully. "If she knows nothing of my past, that does not mean she knows nothing of your history."

"Perhaps," I remarked. "It is worth speaking to her about it."

"You must speak to her," she said. "Fate itself is leading you down this path."

"And what about you?" I asked, understanding that she was right.

"I will move on. The world is vast, and there are a great many places I have not yet been. I want to go north. They say that beyond the seas there are other lands too. Covered in ice, inhabited by quite different peoples."

In the morning we left Ker-Is, heading through the forest to the magical barrier that separated Irene from the rest of the world. The guards let us through unhindered, and a letter I had sent would carry news of my departure to the king. I did not know how long I would be away.

At last parting became inevitable: the road forked, and our paths too had to diverge. Mine led south, to Ulrir; hers led north, to the Kanian ports on the coast.

We embraced.

"Promise me," she said, "that some day you will fulfil a request of mine."

"My House, in my person, swears upon its honour. Whatever may happen, neither gods, nor elements, nor the spirits of the afterlife shall stop me from fulfilling my duty," I bowed ceremoniously before her, and she burst out laughing. And so we parted.

## 23 December, year 2788 since the Creation of the World

Perhaps I ought to tell of my journey to the tower of Rahl-Ulrir, of my first meeting with the Great Sorceress Maeve and of the details of our conversation; there are, however, things that should not be entrusted to paper.

Only this matters: she invited me to become her apprentice. Well, I must admit that I myself had been considering asking one of the Great Mages to take me as a pupil, but I could not even dream that such an offer would come from someone who sits on the Council of the Conclave. Here an explanation is in order: there are only seven such mages, though the number of Great Mages themselves is far larger.

Rahl-Ulrir is one of the Towers of the Great Mages, each of which bears the name of the region in which it stands, and each of which stands at a crossing of the ley lines that girdle our world. Naturally, a tower can only be built on solid ground, so each such crossing has in the end acquired its tower, except perhaps the most remote and awkwardly placed ones.

The word "Rahl" itself translates as "magic tower". The word comes from one of the New Elven tongues, to whose extraordinary popularity we owe a multitude of modern names and titles. A group of elven poets and writers, even before the Change, concerned themselves with "the beauty of language" and, deeming our ordinary speech insufficiently elegant, zealously set about inventing languages of their own, each more intricate than the last.

The fashion for them spread extremely widely, touching not only elves but humans too. Hence all these ornate names and titles, sometimes devoid of any meaning.

Rahl-Ulrir is the closest of the magic towers to Irene, in effect barring the approaches to it. South of it stands Rahl-Ullah, and beyond that begin the Kanian lands. The story of how these towers came to be is extraordinary. Nothing of the kind existed in the times before the Change; however, when the elves awoke and set about exploring the world anew, they came upon a number of towers located in the centre of the continent. Some of them could in time be entered, but nothing could be learned either about who had raised them or for what purpose. Over time, however, artefacts of extraordinary power were found hidden in the towers. It was suggested that these structures had been raised by the June just before their downfall, but in their architecture the towers resembled nothing they had built before. What is more, each of them had been created in a style of its own, utterly unlike the others.

About a dozen towers were found in all; the entrances to some of them had been broken open even before the elves found them, but most remained intact. It was learned that their walls were protected by unusual enchantments that made the towers highly resistant to outside influence. All this led each member of the Conclave to hasten to occupy a Rahl of their own and begin studying it systematically. Over time the number of mages grew, and then they began building towers of their own, in the image and likeness of these.

Rahl-Ulrir, as it happens, is one of the Rahls that existed from the very beginning. I find it most curious to be here; though I know that over the past centuries it has been explored from top to bottom, it seems to me that it still hides some secrets, some unsolved riddles...

A few words about its mistress: the Great Sorceress is very wise, though from her appearance one cannot tell that she is much older than anyone I have known before. She belongs to a branch of the long-vanished House of Morran, about which almost no records have survived.

After I had been in the tower for several weeks, she honoured me with a conversation and informed me that my training would begin very soon. And though I am ready for new knowledge, I understand that in such a matter patience is what counts.

For now all that remains to me is to explore the tower itself and its library. There are not so many other elves here, and among the servants of our Mistress I have met humans too. If I understand correctly, many of Maeve's former pupils now reside in other elven domains. Alas, until now I have taken little interest in present-day politics, being busy with my archive, and besides, almost no news reaches Irene. My kinsfolk are securely sheltered by the barrier from all the sorrows of the outside world, and they care nothing for what happens in it. But, as far as I now know, the Conclave is in fact actively involved in current politics, working together with human mages.

It only remains to learn more about what has so far been unknown to me. Perhaps the present state of affairs will allow me to better understand the events of the past.

## 20 December, year 2689 since the Creation of the World

Well, a year has passed since the beginning of my training, and I can admit that I have truly achieved a great deal in this time. The most magnificent thing of all, of course, must be acknowledged to be my acquaintance with Maeve herself, this enchanting sorceress, as though stepped out of the times that still draw me to them even now. Feeling like a backward warrior of ancient hosts, I understand perfectly those who in their day committed follies for the sake of her cornflower-blue eyes and golden locks.

Once my people were driven by the idea of beauty, and at the very beginning of their history they would not accept any compromise. Striving for absolute perfection, they created magic, having learned the hidden secrets of this world. Before the Change, magic was the lot of the very best; the selection was strict, and the punishment for a mistake was death.

The elves strove to change the world, ridding it of all Ugliness. It is no wonder that my kinsmen of that epoch surpass many times over those of us who came after them. And my teacher is, of course, the embodiment of all the virtues one could expect of an elf of those times.

Together with Maeve we delved into the secrets of higher magic, even into such forbidden branches as the magic of the mind or necromancy. Such knowledge is necessary above all to counter other mages who practise such arts. In Irene there are strict prohibitions against dark magic, but here, in the rest of the world, the restrictions are much weaker. As my teacher explained, only recently the Conclave faced a situation in which a number of mages from among the humans turned against their own kind. Some power had taken hold of them, and only the efforts of the entire Conclave made it possible to deal with them. Now my teacher and the other Great Mages are busy deciding exactly which knowledge should be passed on to others and which must be placed under strict prohibition.

The greatest trust has been placed in me in that I have been allowed to assist the Council of the Conclave in this work. Now, when the unity of the Council has been shattered by the apostasy of the human mage Nezeb, we must all be on our guard.

## 5 September, year 2690 since the Creation of the World

How remarkable: I have now arrived in the lands of humans, to study under the Great Mage Skrakan, lord of Skytower. The road to this forest country was rather long, though fairly safe. The Kingdom of Umoir is one of the many human domains that only formally submit to the authority of Emperor Valir. As far as I know, several elven Houses have also found refuge in Skrakan's lands, so it will be most interesting for me to talk with my kinsfolk. Perhaps what I manage to learn from humans and from elves far removed from Irene will allow me to complete my "Chronicles of Times Past".

Skrakan is an amazing man. In appearance he is already advanced in years, as is typical of humans, who age slowly over the course of their lives; yet, like the other Great Mages, he is very wise and observant. He at once grasped the essence of my requests and was most benevolently disposed towards me throughout our conversation. Skrakan told me the substance of the matter on which Maeve had sent me to him. Originally, after the war with the orcs, the human mages took on many pupils, wishing to increase the number of Great Mages quickly; over time, however, the shortcomings of this approach became clear.

Now the Conclave intends to hold an assembly to work out new rules for those whom the members of the Conclave teach. It seems each Great Mage will be allowed to teach no more than one pupil at a time. In addition, obtaining the very title of Great Mage will be made harder, and the test a candidate must pass will become more difficult.

Skrakan showed me his astronomical instruments. The old man is greatly taken with the problem of studying the so-called "outer worlds", and, if I understand him correctly, he believes that there is some connection between our world and others. At Ardebrig such theories were considered purely speculative, but Skrakan supports his version with certain observations. A curious picture emerges from his charts: it seems that our pole star and the constellation of twelve stars surrounding it may be linked to the vectors of the field of ley lines that converge at the poles of our world.

He could say more precisely only once he had fitted out an expedition to one of the large islands lying in the polar region. That archipelago is close enough to the point in question; such an undertaking, however, requires long and thorough preparation. It is inhabited by very unusual races whose bodies are covered with fur, and the animals there are much larger and more dangerous than those that live on Yul.

Alas, his present affairs do not allow him to take up the question. The human Conclave needs guidance as never before.

## 7 January, year 2743 since the Creation of the World

My work devoted to the history of the elves is finished. History itself, however, is not finished, and therefore we still have something to tell. Though the Kingdom of Irene has frozen in drowsy oblivion, there are still many other states, both human, beginning with the Empire of Kania itself, and elven, founded by those who left their native lands.

Under the wise guidance of the Conclave, in which the mages of elves and humans alike have united, these states may in future achieve a great deal.

I too am now numbered among the Great Mages, for I have passed the test, performed all the necessary rituals and become the owner of a tower of my own.

Rahl-Ney lies in a fertile valley in the mountains. The mountains of Gipat separate it from the main body of the Kanian domains, and these parts have only begun to be settled. Of the previous owners only ruins remain, among them one of the still-working portals that link the former provinces of the June state.

The tower itself was built by Kanians, but it is quite convenient for my purposes. First of all, I ordered that all the manuscripts I had collected be brought here. It still remained to send someone to Irene to make copies of documents in the royal library. Perhaps I too will need pupils, but I have not yet seen suitable candidates.

My musings about future plans were interrupted by the arrival of unexpected guests. The Great Mage Tensess was known to me, but I had never met his companion. Inviting them into the guest chambers, I prepared myself for an interesting conversation.

Tensess is one of Skrakan's pupils and is in effect the head of Kania. And although formally all power belongs to Emperor Valir, the voice of the Great Mage of Kania has always been decisive in settling any question. Tensess went straight to the point:

"As you already know," he said, after the usual ceremonies of greeting, when we had settled at a comfortable table, "Skrakan once had two pupils. Myself and Nezeb. Nezeb was like a brother to me, but his lust for power and his unwillingness to come to terms with others forced me into the duel everyone knows of. He left me no choice, and after his defeat he was exiled to the southern deserts. We are watching him in secret."

Of course, I knew of the memorable duel between the two human Great Mages. Conflicts like this one had occurred among the elves too; it was not for nothing that the first schism in the Council took place even before humans became full members of it.

"Nezeb has found a great deal in the lands of the south," said Tensess's companion, whom I had never seen before, joining the conversation. "Those parts concealed some very remarkable creatures. Jinn, and not only them. The tribes with which Nezeb has allied himself now worship him, and he in turn has taught them magic and created a Conclave of his own."

For some time I wondered who this mysterious companion might be. She wore a long grey cloak with a wide hood, and her face remained in shadow.

"Nezeb has not given up his dreams of power. I wager that sooner or later he will try to return to Kania. This time as a conqueror," Tensess shook his head. "Sevia and I," he indicated his companion, "have long considered what to do. Nezeb must not gain power over Kania. Perhaps we should cede him part of the lands. Let him play the wise ruler and solve his subjects' problems himself. Seeing how he rules, even his most devoted supporters here, in Kania, will abandon him."

"Part of the lands, together with those who live on them?" I was, to be honest, surprised. "I do not think they would wish to find themselves under a conqueror's rule. Is there truly no way to stop Nezeb?"

"War is inevitable," Tensess sighed. "And however much I regret it, Nezeb can hardly be stopped at our borders. But once he invades the Empire of Kania, he will be forced to leave garrisons in the cities he captures, which will certainly weaken him. Besides, I have no other means of uniting the Kanians themselves. Only when they feel a threat to their own domains will they act together. There is no other way, and so we shall have to sacrifice the few for the good of the many."

For some time I pondered this idea. It would never have occurred to my countrymen, though for the most part those who remained living in Irene had never been interested in those who lived beyond the barrier.

"Nezeb," Sevia went on, "is still gathering his armies. He is immortal, and therefore in no hurry. We can prepare, and though Valir is not ready to listen to us, the other Great Mages will prove, at the decisive moment, to be the force that stops him. We have a difficulty, however, and that is why we decided to turn to you. There is something Nezeb must not obtain. I speak of an artefact of extraordinary power that was hidden in one of the towers."

I did of course already know of these artefacts; indeed, I had even held one of them in my hands: the Key of Creation, carefully guarded by my teacher Maeve. The Radiant Beacon had been entrusted to Oberon; Skrakan himself had the Stone Flower; I know too that one of these artefacts was found far to the east, in the lands of the orcs, where some of my kinsfolk had settled. Two keys were now considered lost.

And now another one has been found in the lands of the south. I had always supposed that there were more of these magical objects, for some towers had already been broken into when my awakened ancestors discovered them.

"You think that with this artefact Nezeb will become much stronger?" I asked.

"Other such objects have caused us a great deal of trouble," Tensess remarked. "In a sense, I am even glad we are rid of them. Rada and Rod, their obsession, the powers available to them... All of it is frightening. And the cause of it all was the artefacts they obtained. They must be handled as carefully as possible. And Nezeb... was never careful."

With that I could only agree. Skrakan's pupil was known as a dangerous madman whose plans were ambitious and whose means of achieving his ends were not always clean.

"The artefact must be taken out of the southern lands before Nezeb and his pupils find it," the Great Mage of Kania continued. "I want you to go there, to the lands of the south, and bring this artefact to me. Sevia will go with you; she knows the domains of my former friend well. I think the Conclave can trust you. There is now one vacant seat on the Council, Nezeb's seat, and you could have it."

## 8 January, year 2743 since the Creation of the World

We left Rahl-Ney at dawn. Mighty lions, creatures of magic, carried us forward. The way was long, but I hoped that the ancient June gates would help us shorten it: by my calculations one of the portals led somewhere into the desert, right into the heart of Nezeb's domains.

The June Mountains are endless chains of peaks stretching through the centre of the continent, separating east from west and north from south. Snow-white ridges alternate with green valleys, in one of which my new home stood. It is here that all the great rivers are born, and many caves lie hidden at the roots of the mountains. How unlike Irene, covered in bright forests, where there is nothing higher than small hills and the cliffs on the coast.

For a while we were silent, but then I decided to address my companion, about whom I still knew nothing.

"You are not one of the Great Mages," I remarked cautiously, wondering how to begin this conversation.

"How observant of you. What gave me away, I wonder?" Her voice was full of the most venomous sarcasm.

Well, I had not expected her to answer directly.

"If you know Nezeb's domains so well, then it follows that the southerners trust you and do not know you are Tensess's spy."

"Perhaps in truth I am Nezeb's spy?"

I peered into her calm grey eyes, which expressed nothing.

"You are joking," I said calmly.

"Truth is relative. If you love history so much, you ought to know that."

"Truth is absolute. Something either happened or it did not," I objected without much thought.

"Well, in time you will be disappointed. Chronicles lie, like everyone around. History is written so that it has its heroes and villains, but in life there are neither heroes nor villains," Sevia said this rather indifferently, but I fancied I heard some hidden bitterness in her words.

"A fitting opinion for... a spy," I objected again, beginning to seethe.

She was silent for a while.

"Well, you have probably heard of the end of the war with the orcs."

"When Tensess and Nezeb killed Skulnar?"

"Tensess and Nezeb stood by the camp and waited. I was the one who killed him."

"You?!" I was indeed somewhat stunned.

"Imagine it: I crawled on my belly to the tent, killed the sentries with blows from behind, then slit the wall of the yurt, went in, found a fat old orc and cut his throat. Not very heroic, is it?"

"The chronicles really do describe it differently," I remarked, still doubtful.

"Because people do not need the truth, they need heroes. Pretty fairy tales in which good triumphs over evil. The real thing... is usually not very pretty."

"And yet the orcs themselves believe that Skulnar vanished."

"His little son was very afraid that the division of the inheritance would get him knifed next. So he handed his father's body over to the shamans. They, in turn, preferred to bury it somewhere in secret. The Nomadic clan owned a great many sea vessels, and the body was carried off on them."

"Where to?"

"That I do not know; by that time nobody cared about them. The Horde was at each other's throats."

While I was thinking what else to ask her, we were already approaching the portal. The rest was up to me: activating it required considerable effort. That is why portals cannot let whole armies through and serve only as a means of dire need. Such was ours.

## 25 March, year 2743 since the Creation of the World

We left our lions on the other side of the portal: they were intelligent enough to return to the tower on their own, but here, in the desert, they were useless. Sevia was to obtain some means of transport for us, with which a long journey lay ahead.

All I could do was wait for her not far from the small town near which the portal stood. Of course, I could have gone with her, disguised by an illusion, but there was always the risk of running into one of Nezeb's pupils, and I did not know the limits of their abilities. There were also the mysterious jinn Sevia had spoken of.

Some couple of hours later she returned with two unusually ugly creatures, somewhat resembling humpbacked horses. Noticing my puzzled look, she handed me the reins.

"Camels, the best means of travelling through the desert."

Well, there was nothing left for me but to clamber onto this creature and meekly follow my companion. For the umpteenth time I wondered whether I could trust her, and whether she was not leading me into a trap. Under torture Nezeb could extract a great deal from me about the workings of the Conclave. But Tensess trusted Sevia...

As we rode, I cast cautious glances at her. My companion had the most ordinary human appearance. Unlike Bindweed, who was as beautiful as late spring, Sevia's face I would not have recognised in a crowd, so ordinary and unremarkable was it. Hair of some mousy colour, narrow, pursed and almost colourless lips, grey eyes.

Was she close to Tensess? That I could not say for certain. The trusting nature of their relationship, however, spoke volumes.

A sweltering desert: that is the essence of the whole south and of the lands that now make up the domains of the former pupil, Nezeb. Of course, far to the west lie marshy bogs, but the entire south-east is endless dunes mixed with scorched stony wastelands. The way from the portal to our goal was scorching, and we could travel only at night, when the blazing ball of the sun hid below the horizon.

Sevia masterfully led me from one shelter to the next. Her maps held notes on oases, desert wells, everything one needs to survive in this inhospitable land.

## 29 March, year 2743 since the Creation of the World

We passed the dunes of Arav and went deep into the stony wastes of Kandar. A sinister place, full of wind-hewn rocks in which the passing simoom raised doleful howls that frightened the natives to death.

However, though at first I had hoped to cross this stretch of the way in safety, it quite soon became clear to me that my companion by no means considered it safe. Sevia carefully examined every strange shadow, every turn.

"Ghouls," she muttered through her teeth when my interest became obvious.

Strange; I myself had not sensed any presence of the dead in this area. Ghouls were indeed dangerous, especially in large numbers. These morphed members of the undead were considered something to be avoided whenever possible. Rather late, I remembered that Kandar had in its time been considered a cursed place. Even before the transformation of the elves, necromancy had flourished here, and the warlocks of ancient Hickut had waged wars against one another.

The outcome of their battles, in which they finally slaughtered one another, was armies of undead that obeyed no one and began slowly to creep out of Kandar into the surrounding lands. Only the newly created Conclave managed to stop this threat.

It had seemed to me that the Council, which at that time consisted only of elves, had dealt with the rampant undead once and for all. But it turned out that someone had remained...

My reflections on the Conclave's responsibility for what was happening were rudely interrupted by attacking ghouls. Before I could blink an eye, the gorge seemed to boil with the misshapen bodies of these creatures.

Sevia, drawing a short blade, shouted something, but I did not make out what... My spells were already in motion: with a practised gesture I raised a wall of fire that cut off most of the enemies, then at once brought down a hail of stone upon the rest. The rout was completed by a cloud of the strongest acid, from which smoke poured off the nearest stones. The ghouls, realising that before them were not merchants who had decided to take a short cut, immediately made themselves scarce. With my next movement I created a powerful gust of wind that put out the fire and dispersed the poisonous cloud.

Turning to my companion, I noticed a slight surprise on her face, which she immediately tried to hide.

Putting away her blade, she mounted her camel without a word and rode on. Smiling to myself, I followed her. Apparently the ghouls had sense enough not to pursue us any further, and by sunset we had crossed the mountains onto yet another waste.

"Presumably," I tried after all to start a conversation, "these are not the only undead one can meet here."

Sevia was silent for some time, then said:

"Not the only ones. But they are not all one should fear."

She launched into a long talk about the creatures of the south. Siranises, albasty, mirages and karkadanns... After a while our conversation turned to something else.

"Tensess and Nezeb are ice and fire, water and sand. Different in everything, they could have remained the best of friends. But there was something that divided them."

"Someone," I guessed.

"Right. I could be with one of them, but not with both at once. In the end it was power that divided them, but the first crack appeared thanks to me."

I honestly did not know what to say to her. These Kanian intrigues seemed to me a very tangled business. Sevia looked at it from her own side, but probably the truth was a little more complicated. And yet, out of what trifles the stream of history is made...

Meanwhile my companion switched to our coming goal:

"They call this tower the 'Pillar of Fire'. Nezeb has already tried to get at it and left empty-handed. He posted guards whom I will not be able to persuade to let us through. Fortunately, he himself is no longer in these lands. His presence was needed elsewhere, so we have a chance to get what we want."

By the time the sun set, we were beyond Kandar. Ahead lay the lands of the Zem people, and from the top of the plateau on which Sevia and I stood, one could see the long ribbon of the Eter dividing the desert. The tower we needed was somewhere there, among dead ruins.

We stopped for our last night's camp. Less than a day to our goal, and no one can predict what awaits us there. Nezeb had left guards, but neither their number nor their makeup was known.

I spread out my cloak and lay down on the stony ground, gazing at the stars on high. My eyes found the constellation Skrakan had spoken of. Curious. I wonder how the study of the stars drove the Great Mages mad? My reflections were rudely interrupted by Sevia, who suddenly flopped down on top of me and fastened her lips on mine in a kiss. In my surprise I almost pushed her away, but restrained myself in time. Her lips were salty, like the sands of the deserts. Only the stars on high were watching us.

## 30 March, year 2743 since the Creation of the World

In the morning she got up and, as usual, began quickly getting ready. In answer to my embarrassed look, she only shrugged.

"Hurry, we need to reach the Pillar of Fire as quickly as possible."

We continued on our way. If until that day I had hardly come across any ruins of the Hickut civilisation, this river valley was lined with them. As far as I understood, until now there had been very few willing to profit from what remained after the death of their civilisation. But for Nezeb nothing was forbidden. He had appropriated no man's land and everything on it.

The past night made me see the relations between Sevia and Nezeb a little differently. That complicated knot of contradictions, entwined with Tensess, now included me as well. But what does my companion really want, and whom does she serve?

There had been no shortage of mysterious girls in my life, such as Bindweed, but Sevia... And if Bindweed truly did not know who she was, Sevia was hiding far too much.

Even now one could only guess: what exactly does she want? Is she a double or a triple agent? Is she loyal to Tensess, or acting in Nezeb's interests? Why would she hand this dangerous artefact over to us? Perhaps we are meant to destroy ourselves by using it?

I knew nothing for certain, but I was prepared in advance for any surprises. Before leaving the camels and moving on, I spent an hour enchanting myself and Sevia, making us completely invisible and inaudible to any ordinary people. Only one of the Great Mages could detect us.

We walked through ruins whose inhabitants had been dead for several centuries now. In this dead city, Sar-Iram, once one of the capitals of Hickut, it was unusually quiet, and, as they say, even the beasts gave it a wide berth.

Of course, no curse can frighten off greedy people with a weakness for treasure. And traces of the thieves' work were everywhere. Plundering everything of the slightest value, they were gradually reducing the history of this place to nothing. Somewhere in the distance we saw huge pyramids looming over the rest of the city. It seemed that they alone would outlive the coming centuries.

At last the tower appeared before my eyes; slowly but surely its top began to rise above the houses and the mounds of sand that were gradually burying the streets.

"The Pillar of Fire," Sevia pronounced almost solemnly when, riding up yet another hill, we saw it whole, from top to bottom. Around the tower, which stood in the middle of a square, tents could be seen, and around them people swarmed like ants: guards from the tribes that had sworn allegiance to Nezeb.

"What shall we do?" I asked.

"Wait," Sevia muttered. "These dolts are too careless. Nezeb should have taken my people."

She was right: soon after sunset the camp had mostly fallen asleep, and the sentries they had posted were chatting carelessly with one another.

Slowly but surely we moved towards the tower. Its gates were broken: it seemed that Nezeb himself had not long ago smashed the old stones to rubble. But, as I understood, he had not managed to find the main thing.

As soon as we entered, Sevia at once turned off somewhere to the side, drawing me after her. We walked through endless corridors, now descending, now climbing stairs again. Without my companion I would very quickly have got lost, but she knew where to go.

At last, after yet another turn, we came up against a dead end.

Sevia at once began running her hands over the bas-relief and, having evidently felt something, pressed a spring mechanism invisible to me. The stone wall trembled, sand poured down, and then the seemingly immovable monolith did after all begin to turn, letting us into the inner room.

I immediately felt the radiance emanating from the artefact that lay in the very centre of the hall. That powerful magical aura pierced even my protection.

Now it was up to me. Having conjured a multitude of shields, I slowly began drawing the treasure towards me. To my surprise, no traps were triggered. Anyone who came in here could have taken this object.

Seizing the hot object in my hands, I at once hid it in my shoulder bag. Without delay we hurried to the tower's exit. Alas, what followed was not so simple, and as soon as I crossed the threshold I heard an extraordinarily loud roar.

"A jinn!" was all my companion shouted. Nezeb's servants, armed with curved yataghans, were already running towards us from the camp.

Once again I conjured a shield, protecting myself from a lightning bolt sent by the jinn, and feverishly began to think what to do next. The jinn was strong. I supposed that I could still deal with it, but that would take time, and who knows whether it might not summon its friends here, and Nezeb along with them?

Fortunately, I was spared having to fight the others as well: Sevia, covering her face, stepped out to meet them. Without hesitation she threw herself at two dozen men. I could not follow her movements: Sevia moved incredibly fast, with smooth, flowing motions. Her blades struck unerringly, the honed edges cutting down the guards and leaving them no chance.

I repelled another attack from the jinn roaring somewhere on high, and involuntarily reached with my magical sight towards my bag. The artefact, reacting to our battle, had grown hot as a coal from a campfire. A stream of energy was pouring from it, so easy to scoop up...

Involuntarily I did so, and was myself horrified at what happened. A discharge of the pure energy of the primal elements burned the jinn to ashes and raised a sandstorm around us. But at the same time I immediately felt the gazes of the other Great Mages turn towards me. Surprised, bewildered, angry. Nezeb was among them. We had very little time.

From the artefact stretched a magical thread invisible to the eye, leading somewhere to the north. To Skytower, it seemed. Excellent. Grasping the hand of Sevia, who could barely stand in the raging whirlwind of sand, I scooped up as much power as I could and cast a spell of transference, guiding myself by the magical thread.

## 16 May, year 2743 since the Creation of the World

It is hard even to imagine the might of the artefact that lay before me. As soon as I touched it with spells, everything around seemed to start ringing, shuddering with the might locked in this scarlet stone. Unknown forces, it seemed, had enclosed the whole might of a primal element in a tiny grain, as though at some moment it was to open, releasing what was locked within. The potential might was alluring. The Great Dragons must have possessed such at the zenith of their flourishing. I tried to concentrate and, using certain techniques from the arsenal of the oracles, created a mental double of myself, which in turn reached out with the reflection of my mind towards the "Grain of the Primal Element".

I saw the artefact as though woven from a multitude of the finest threads; its materiality was only apparent, and in reality it was nothing but embodied power. I wondered: did my teacher see the same? And the other Great Mages? Looking more closely, I saw that some of the threads stretched away, somewhere into the incredible depths of our world. Following them with my double's gaze, I saw an even larger tangle, hidden in a space that itself seemed to have been crumpled and folded many times over. Like a sheet of paper folded again and again. I was afraid even to imagine what power the tangle itself held, for each thread woven into it contained more magic than the entire Conclave of Great Mages could use. This incredible power belonged to no one. The threads entwined the ley lines that converged and crossed at the places where the tangles lay. It all resembled a huge net thrown over our world.

My research was interrupted by Tensess coming in. He had been staying at Skytower for quite some time, remaining even after Sevia had coldly taken leave of us both and gone off somewhere.

"Incredible," I said to him after a while.

The Great Mage smiled.

"One of the mysteries of our world. And no one knows where they came from."

"Someone gave us incredible power. Just like that. Asking nothing in return?"

"You speak my words. I fear that one day we will be called to account for this debt. With interest."

I nodded in agreement.

"Knowing what happened to Rod and Rada, knowing what happened to Kanaan, I think it is better for us to leave them. Hide them. Conceal them more securely. Until we decide that we are ready. And if we now stand on the threshold of war with Nezeb, all the more reason why this means must not be used as a weapon. We will return to it when peace comes. No matter how long we have to wait."

## Irene

Oh, that famous story, directly bound up with Irene! Once, the last kingdom of the elves stood here. During the Cataclysm it survived thanks to an unusual artifact kept by King Grallon – the Key of Creation. And the king had a daughter, the young Princess Daguta, who could never find herself a suitor…

All was well until a mysterious Stranger, guided by aims and designs of his own, appeared at the castle gates! He seduced Daguta, forced her to steal the Key, and so doomed everyone!

King Grallon managed to escape with a handful of courtiers, and they watched Irene sink into the depths of the Astral. But, as we now know, the allod was not destroyed completely after all…

Once the elves had a single kingdom – Irene. After the fall of the June nothing could compare with the might of this kingdom, in which even the lowliest vagabond wielded magic. Striving to become stronger still, the elite of this elven kingdom delved ever deeper into realms of magic unexplored until then.

The attention of the elves was drawn to the mysterious magic of the June, blood magic. Through the rituals of blood magic, some elves became vampires and were doomed to an eternal thirst that could only be quenched with the blood of others. These events came to be known as the "Blood Feast".

The problem that arose was eventually brought to naught, but it did not pass without a trace for Irene: trust among the elves had been destroyed. Many of them left the bounds of the kingdom and settled in various hidden corners of Yul. A little later the elves began to form Houses, family clans, each of which lived by its own laws and rules.

## Ammer

An allod born after the death of two gods. Both fell in a cruel battle. The energy released at the moment of their death was so great that it pierced the whole world and took shape as the Well of Souls. The Astral hastily retreated from it, allowing a new allod to grow out of nothing. A few days later the first Aoidoi were born. The plants and animals here possess colossal vitality and develop in an utterly chaotic way.

## Ark

There was one place in Sarnaut where the enmity between Kania and Xadagan did not matter. A remarkable place it was – the allod of Ark, ruled since olden times by the Great Mage Erast. The valley in which Erast's domain lay is an extraordinarily beautiful spot. Small rivers flowed down from the mountains, and everything around was planted with gardens full of roses.

Ark was originally a small principality in the far south-west of Kania. Nezeb's conquest, when he unleashed the hordes of Ugra upon the southern borders, passed it by, but at the same time cut it off from the main body of the Kanian lands.

Erast himself considered himself independent, but he did pay Nezeb various marks of respect – he was, after all, his nearest neighbour. The Xadaganian emperor, for his part, did not dare to touch Ark either: the profits of trade were considerable, and there would be no benefit in simply seizing such a scrap of land.

If one were to choose a place to live as one pleased, Ark might well have been it. Neither Kania nor Xadagan collected taxes or recruited troops there: live and let live. All the more so as there were hardly any threats on Ark… Except perhaps for a few trolls and kobolds in the mountain caves, but they did not risk coming down into the valley. And the people of Ark were, of course, a cheerful lot. Kanians and Xadaganians had long since mingled here, and one could no longer tell them apart. Elves also lived in these lost lands – the House de Ark.

## Gelida

A rather… harsh place, an island of eternal winter, although the local forests are full of all kinds of beasts, and the rivers and lakes are full of fish.

## Grok

A vast steppe; small forests and mountains are found here only at the edges of the island.

Originally the allod belonged to the elves of the House de Vevre, who had several small towns here. Admittedly, the local steppes are not very fertile – there are few rivers, cold winds often blew, so grain did not grow very well either. Magic helped the elves with this, and besides magic they found another solution: breeding all manner of livestock.

But there was one misfortune on Grok that constantly disturbed the peaceful life of the elves. And the name of that misfortune was orcs. There were countless orcs here, and they lived in the steppes, a little further from the centre of the allod. The House de Vevre, of course, would have liked to be rid of the orcs – but how do you chase them across the steppes?

Everything changed in the year 707 of the New Era, when the orcs and the Xadaganians captured Grok, killing Claude de Vevre, the Great Mage of the allod. Nezeb kept the promise he had given Rodogor, and the allod came to be held by a Xadaganian Great Mage.

An expedition of historians sent out (recently) managed to find part of the documents from the archive of the Great Mage Mark, which had survived on one of the shards of the destroyed allod.

As it turned out, the Empire had found elven documents describing events connected with the Great Orc. In the days when the allod was still held by an elven Great Mage, an unusual child was born into the tribe of orcs that lived on Grok – Lorzub...

The Xadaganians who found the records of the elven Great Mage Claude de Vevre all the more preferred to hide from everyone the fact that such an orc had really existed, not wishing to give the shamans hope of finally breaking away from the Empire. But now the legacy of the Legendary Orc has returned to the world – who knows what it will lead to?

One of the legends passed in a whisper from mothers to children is the tale of an orc who wielded magic. Time has erased the details of this story – no one can even say for certain on which of the allods it happened, or when. But the legend lives its own life – and gives hope to the shamans, who have long wished to throw off the yoke of the Empire's Great Mages and declare the allod of Izune free.

The Xadaganians themselves consider this claim entirely unconfirmed. In their view, the magical abilities that occasionally appear among orcs of the Fierce clan are the result of astral mutation. Additional data could have come from a study of the allod from which Skulnar's ancestors hail – Grok – but that allod is now lost, torn apart by astral demons during their first deadly attack.

It remains only to wonder: what if the Legendary Orc is no accident, no blind play of fate, but someone's creation? Who possesses a power capable of transforming a living being in such a way? And for what purpose was this deed done?

## Igsh

## Lightwood

Wintry. Coniferous forests. Representatives of the House de Craner have now opened a fencing school on the allod of Lightwood, where you can meet elves as well as Kanians and Gibberlings!

## Yoggor

Yoggor – once the domain of the House de Doucer…

The Great Mage of this allod was the wise Gramont de Doucer, a pupil of the elven mages of antiquity, only slightly inferior in power to Skrakan. He gathered everyone who found themselves on his allod after the Night of Woe into one single great House and revived the tradition of the Great Houses, in which the remaining Eight Great Houses now began to take part.

Yoggor itself is a rather unusual place, a majestic forest full of enormous trees. Most of the elves live in their own castles, scattered in great numbers across the allod. Although only elves inhabit this allod, there are also those here capable of posing a threat to lone travellers – various mindless creatures such as giant spiders and mantises. But everything comes to an end, and so a terrible fate befell Yoggor as well – an extraordinarily deadly spell that changed the usual way of life on the allod, shrouding it in darkness.

## Xadagan

The lands that now lie within the allod of Xadagan are considered the centre of the Zem civilisation. Before the sands swallowed the ancient ruins, the state of Hickut existed here, in the river valley. When the Zem were wiped out by the plague, the old irrigation systems were destroyed, and only a few oases gave shelter to the peoples of Ugra, who roamed the desert and came to replace the builders of the pyramids.

But then the Cataclysm destroyed the pyramids, which had been traps for Sparks, and the Arisen returned, quite literally, from the other world. Over the millennia the world had changed a great deal and was far from friendly towards them – at first all that awaited them was either death or slavery in the mines.

The Zem had to work hard to win back their lands – in the end a compromise was found. Nefer Ur, formerly the Chief Mechanic of the Zem people, became the Great Mage, the keeper of the allod of Xadagan.

Much has changed on this allod since then: the Zem have transformed it according to their own tastes and needs. Old buildings dug out of the sand stand side by side with brand-new structures sparkling with the lights of modern technology. To many Xadaganians this look seems too mechanical and lifeless, but for the rational Zem it is just what is needed. Today the Arisen are ready to act in alliance with the other races of the Empire.

## Malar

A very peaceful allod, inhabited since the most ancient times, when Kania was a single state rather than a collection of separate islands. Usually nothing happens here; even the demons hardly ever attacked. There are no large cities, but a great many small villages and farmsteads. Vast forests, in which a stranger can very easily lose his way.

## Ney

Ney is not a very large allod, although it was here that Zayan, together with Skrakan, first succeeded in creating the Stasis ritual. It lies in the middle of a plain that was once high in the mountains. The local landmark deserves a mention too – Rakhl-Ney, a tower that is almost the only building on the allod. Today the Council of Historians sits in it. The tower itself is a grandiose library, with shelves the size of several houses.

Of course, it is not only books that are kept in Rakhl-Ney: there are plenty of different artifacts here as well.

Besides the tower itself, the sights here include an old system of portals leading to a great many allods. This was something like a crossroads where many of the magical paths of the June tribe converged… It is only a pity that many of the portals no longer work.

## Heart of Fire

[It seems the entries in this diary are more than five years old. You open Arat's diary and read]:

Verily, there is no one in the world more perfect than dragons. I have always striven to understand them. Alas, in our time it is rather hard to meet dragons… For many years I searched for them. I honed my skills and abilities and gained new knowledge. I read the manuscripts of long-dead elven magisters on the ruins of long-destroyed allods…

At last I became the best in my trade. I am hired by Great Mages who desire their Blood. In the blood of dragons lies the greatest power! One day I shall master it completely.

And yesterday I received the contract of my dreams. Lady Catherina, the Great Mage of Umoir, charged me with capturing two dragons. I know where to get what is required: the dragons Soliskar and Agrus, who hid from human eyes after the well-known events in the Dead City. I managed to find out exactly where they retreated with their army of draconids. That place is the island of the Heart of Fire, their old haven, their hidden refuge.

I have a team. Goblins – pitiful, worthless creatures, no loss to anyone. Many of them will die, but they will be able to set the necessary trap.

I will track down and capture the dragons! Catherina has let me in on her plan and granted me a portion of her power. Verily, there is no one in the world more perfect than dragons. It will pain me to sacrifice them. A pity, but we have no other power capable of breaking the Seal and freeing the Creator.

## Stellara

The allod is a serene forest beneath a starry night sky. It is also home to the principal school of magic for elves, where they are sent while still small children. Apart from the elves, the only inhabitants are lamias, whom we teach magic. From them a special "magical support regiment" has now been formed, commanded by a certain mysterious lady.

## Tempesta

A harsh place where a thunderstorm rages constantly, an eternal season of tempests. Our buildings stand on the shore of a huge lake, on sheer cliffs, but we do not complain of the inconvenience, for we have managed to secure ample comfort inside our homes, protected from any bad weather. The local tribe of minotaurs has become our faithful servants and has proved itself excellent at guarding our goods.

## Florenta

A blossoming place where, it seems, there are no seasons but spring and summer. Yes, the whole allod is covered in flowers and shrubs, the scent makes your head spin, and the buzzing of countless bees drowns out every other sound. Harpies also live on the allod, and they have long served the House de Vevre.

## Yakhch

Yakhch was once an ordinary desert allod, but it was here, in their day, that the druids came, having decided to try planting a seed of the Great Tree in one of the oases.

The Tree changed the surrounding landscape of Yakhch enormously. Where there was once desert, mighty forests now rise – a true taiga. The climate changed as well: there is more rainfall, and on the whole it is colder. Now this land is a source of timber, which the Xadaganians ship to various regions of their state.

None of the Great Mages knows what the Great Trees really are. It is believed that the first of them grew somewhere on a northern island, and appeared on Yul noticeably later, when some merchant managed to obtain their seeds. However, in the Era of Allods it turned out that even a small sapling of the Tree can protect a whole city from the Astral.

Even though the power of Tep, who become a personified God of Death, is great, many of his followers have begun doubting Tep's true intentions - and the notion that conquering worlds can bring them happiness. Are they truly ready to cast the world unto absolute predestination while being aware that their fates might be predetermined, or should they trust the infinite possibilities of true randomness of chance?

Can be obtained during seasonal events.

How many wars would all these great heroes have won if they fought on an empty stomach? This is what all the famous chefs think, as warriors eat their meals between battles.

Source: Great Feast Prophetic Card.

On forgotten allods lost in the distant astral plane, lived warrior monks who combined the power of the sword and their faith in the Light. They dedicated their lives to serving it and protecting the world from the dark forces threatening the peace in all of Sarnaut. One day, when the skies darkened with ominous clouds, their wise abbot gathered all the warriors and told them of the impending threat - an army of shadows that sought to devour this world. Inspired by his speech, the monks swore to use their faith as a weapon against evil.

Source: Holy Army Prophetic Card.

Every craftsman on the island of artisans had their own secret, handed down from one generation to the next. The old, long-bearded blacksmith was forging swords and hammers so durable that they were capable of breaking stone. And the wise old lady was weaving wonderful fabrics - shimmering like the starlit sky. There was no quarrel and miscommunication on the island: all the people lived in harmony and helped one another, for each of their handiworks was filled with love and warmth.

Source: Elegant Patterns Prophetic Card.

All wearers of the famous chef's hat protect its secret. Some believe that a mysterious assistant is hidden in it, whispering recipes to the cook.

Source: Great Feast Prophetic Card.

Armed with prayers and sacred symbols, the warrior monks set out into the heart of the dark forest, the Shadow Woods, where creatures of darkness dwelled. Every step along this gloomy path reminded them of their mission - to protect the innocent and restore the true faith. In the forest they encountered terrible monsters, but their faith gave them strength. With each battle, the monks became more confident in their faith, their hearts filled with light, and their swords shone like the sun.

Source: Holy Army Prophetic Card.

In the distant blue Astral sea, beyond seven mountains and nine rivers, was the magical island of the folk craftsmen who arrived here from Kania, a long time ago. Kind experts in their crafts lived there - they knew neither the labors of the factory nor gold, but created miracles with their own hands. Every day they gathered on the verdant glade where the spirits of craftsmanship inspired them to create unique items. They sewed, they wove, they cut and they sculpted - and each of their creations could have become a fairytale in its own right.

Source: Elegant Patterns Prophetic Card.

One day a young pioneer girl named Nastenka, while walking outside the pioneer camp, came across a giant pumpkin growing in an abandoned greenhouse. This wonderful pumpkin glowed golden and enticed her with its sweet aroma. Nastenka, forgetting all the warnings, began to devour its juicy pulp, not realizing that with each bite something terrible was happening to her. The next morning, the pioneers were horrified when they saw Nastenka - her head was now an ugly pumpkin with a smiling mouth and evil eyes. From then on, the girl with the pumpkin head became a scary story that was told to everyone who came to the pioneer camp.

Despite all his efforts, Khitr was unable to find a way to return to earth from the moon. Days turned into years, and years into centuries, and he remained trapped in this strange world. Alone and desperate, he began to forget his past and his purpose. With each passing day, the magic of the moon became more and more powerful, and his mind began to disintegrate under its influence. Eventually, Khitr lost his identity, turning into a mad sorcerer.

Their souls were captured by darkness, and their hearts turned to ice. The necromancer, consumed by his ambitions, could not stop the horror he had caused. The resurrected Marksmen turned on their allies, not distinguishing friend from foe. The bloody battle erupted with renewed vigor.
